newsitem.title: GERMANY: After chiding, Germans wonder if they can reform.
newsitem.headline: After chiding, Germans wonder if they can reform.

text.p: Germans debated on Monday whether Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government can bring about reforms needed for EMU and the globalised economy after President Roman Herzog pleaded with Bonn to end its political logjam.

Herzog, whose largely ceremonial office is above partisan wrangling, scolded the whole political class in a hard-hitting speech on Saturday accusing legislators of failing to tackle long overdue reforms of tax, pension and labour laws.

Kurt Biedenkopf, one of Kohl's longest-standing rivals in the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), got personal by calling the chancellor's plan to run for reelection next year a risk for the party and calling for a primary to pick a candidate.

The only thing most politicians and pundits discussing the weekend's jabs at Kohl agreed on was that Bonn urgently needed to reform its welfare state to be ready for Europe's single currency and stand up to growing competition from abroad.

Talks between the government and the Social Democrat (SPD) opposition on reforming the tax system collapsed last week in a rush of mutual accusations that looked very much like the start of the campaign for the October 1998 election.

Berlin's Tagesspiegel daily said Biedenkopf's criticism was shared outside the small circle of CDU mavericks and added: "Especially for young voters, Kohl is a symbol of immobilism and weak decision making."

Education and Research Minister Juergen Ruettgers defended Bonn's record so far but admitted the country, now suffering record unemployment over four million, had fallen behind its competitors in creating new jobs.

"They all started earlier than we did," he told SWF radio. "This is linked to German reunification. Suddenly the west German market had 17 million new customers, which it served without thinking that structural reforms were needed."

"Who would dispute the fact this country is caught in a web of mutual blockades?" the left-leaning Frankfurter Rundschau daily asked. "The harder question is why this is and how these cramps can be eased."
Herzog, whose speech was widely reprinted in the press, said Germany had to stop moaning about its problems and foster a culture of flexibility and self-reliance.

"We are letting ourselves behave as if we had all the time in the world for change. Whether it's taxes, pensions, health, education or (European) monetary union, all you hear are the voices of the lobby groups and the doubters," he said.
"I warn all concerned against delaying or thwarting any of these reforms for tactical reasons. We cannot afford to have our political institutions blockading themselves."
Rudolf Augstein, publisher of the news weekly Der Spiegel, said Herzog had put his finger on widespread dissatisfaction with the "politics as usual" mood dominating in Bonn.
"He senses an unarticulated will for change that a collosus is blocking," he wrote. "He senses that various groups have a seldom articulated desire to say -- give us anything but this!"
Opinion polls published at the weekend supported the impression of popular discontent and resignation.
Spiegel ran a poll saying 56 percent of respondents were pessimistic about the future and 42 percent doubted either Kohl or the SPD could solve the unemployment problem.
The latest Emnid weekly poll showed a possible SPD-Greens coalition would beat Kohl's centre-right government by 49 to 43 percent if the national election were held now.
At the same time, 54 percent of respondents said they expected Kohl to win reelection next year.

The most popular politician in Spiegel's monthly poll was the SPD's Gerhard Schroeder, the Lower Saxony premier who is competing with SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine to get the party's nod as its challenger to Kohl. Spiegel noted Schroeder has kept out of the Bonn wrangling over tax and pension reforms.

"Schroeder's party, the SPD, is hardly profiting from the popularity of its possible chancellor candidate," the magazine wrote. "Like the CDU, it suffers from voters' growing doubts that politicians can solve today's most important isssues."
